properties.statement:
**ALEX'S TWO MACHINES PRODUCED THE SAME SYMPTOM — "he reported a bug that is already fixed" — BY TWO DIFFERENT MECHANISMS, AND THIS SESSION GOT BOTH WRONG BEFORE MEASURING THEM.**

═══ 🛑 WORK MACHINE (the five hand-typed ideas): HE WAS SIMPLY CORRECT ═══

Alex, 2026-08-14: *"My hand typed observations were using 0.28.0."* Measured against the tags:
```
v0.28.0   2026-08-11      <- what he was running
v0.29.0   2026-08-12
v0.30.0   2026-08-13
fadc197   2026-08-13   PR #172 — write_shareable_export AND detected_indent
```
`git merge-base --is-ancestor fadc197 v0.28.0` → **NO.** **BOTH of the items this session called "already fixed" landed AFTER the version he was running.**

⇒ **HIS REPORTS WERE ACCURATE FOR HIS VERSION. There was no missing committable export and no indent-preserving merge in 0.28.0, because neither existed yet.** This session repeatedly framed those two notes as describing behaviour that no longer exists and inferred a stale user from them. **The inference was backwards: he reported current behaviour, and it was fixed two days later.**

⭐⭐ **AND THE REAL FINDING IS THE CADENCE, NOT THE USER.** Three releases in three days (0.28.0 → 0.29.0 → 0.30.0, 11th to 13th August). **At that rate every user is behind by construction**, and any report they write is against a version that has already moved. `user-iterative-release-preference` asks for BOTH frequent very-minor releases AND a one-word update — **the first without the second guarantees a stream of reports about bugs that are already fixed, and guarantees the maintainer misreads them as staleness.** That is exactly what happened here, all day.

═══ 🛑 HOME MACHINE (the Grok feedback.md): A DIFFERENT MECHANISM ENTIRELY ═══

Alex: *"0.30.0 from home"* — binary current. But the Grok agent measured the project's `.reflow2/kit-version.json` at **0.11.0 / 0ec473e (2026-07-25)** and diagnosed it in its first paragraph: *"the kit sidecar and the process you are talking to are not the same generation."* This session read that as evidence of a stale install; it was evidence of a SPLIT.

`.reflow2/kit-version.json` is written by `reflow2_init.py` INTO the project and records **which kit set that project up**. It is a receipt for an install EVENT, not a live reading. So a binary updated to 0.30.0 leaves a project initialised by kit 0.11.0 exactly where it was — and the fixes that matter to that project (`write_shareable_export`, `detected_indent`) live in `tools/reflow2_init.py`, **a KIT file, not the binary.** Re-running the installer is the only thing that applies them, and nothing says so.

═══ 🛑🛑 WHY THE MAINTAINER CANNOT REPRODUCE THE HOME CASE ═══
```
~/.local/share/reflow2/kit -> /home/ajs7/project/reflow2      A SYMLINK to the checkout
```
while `tools/install.sh` gives a consumer a **tarball extraction** — a frozen copy. **The developer's kit cannot go stale by construction; the consumer's always can.** `req:the-tool-finds-its-own-blind-spots` arriving in the ENVIRONMENT rather than in a detector, and the sharpest instance recorded so far.

═══ WHAT IS AND IS NOT ESTABLISHED ═══

✅ Work machine ran 0.28.0 and its reports were correct for it.
✅ Home binary is 0.30.0; the home project's sidecar was 0.11.0.
⚠️ Whether the home machine's INSTALLED KIT is also old, or only that project's receipt — `reflow2 --version` reports the BINARY and nothing surfaces the kit's version. That is the gap the Grok report's own opportunities section proposed closing.
⚠️ Whether a stale kit costs anything concrete. A 0.11.0 `reflow2_check.py` would predate the LINEAGE (BL-107) and IDENTITY (BL-169) checks, so a consumer's CI gate could be silently weaker than this project's — **not verified.**

⇒ TWO UPDATE SURFACES, ONE UPDATE COMMAND: the binary and the per-project kit. `install.sh` serves the first. A project already set up is served by nothing.
